speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: STARRED QUESTIONS
speechtext:
1.	Has the government any plans for the development of ports and harbours along the route of the seaway?
2.	What is being done at the port of Montreal? Are the plans as announced by the former administration being carried out? What plans are being evolved for the development of the south shore?
3.	Is this area to be taken over by the national harbours board? Are port facilities to be erected here for the expected increase in volume of trade?
4.	What is being done at the port of Trois-Rivieres?
5.	Is consideration being given to the construction of additional wharves and warehouses?
6.	Will the national harbours board provide cargo handling equipment at the port for vertical hatch loading and unloading, extra space on existing wharves and new docks?
7.	Is consideration being given to the construction of a grain elevator here?
8.	What is being done at the port of Sorel?
9.	Will the national harbours board provide cargo handling equipment at the port for vertical hatch loading and unloading, extra space on existing wharves and new docks?
10.	Are port facilities in this area considered adequate for seaway traffic?

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport):
maintopic: STARRED QUESTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in regard to part 1 of the question, perhaps I might give a reply under 96698-36
three headings. First, the national harbours board is giving active consideration to necessary harbour developments at Quebec, Montreal and Three Rivers. I may say I have had the pleasure of visiting all three of these ports and was very much impressed with the facilities now provided and with the plans for improvements and additions. Second, the development and plans for harbours administered by local commissions, that is to say Toronto, Hamilton and Belleville, are the responsibility of those commissions. Here again I was very glad to have an opportunity to visit both Toronto and Hamilton harbours recently and review the program of work to be undertaken at both points. In Toronto both the federal Department of Public Works and the harbour commission are undertaking additional works. At Hamilton the commission has a substantial program of works and, as previously announced, I propose to introduce legislation to authorize a loan to assist these works. In addition funds will be provided to public works to build a new low-level bridge across the harbour entrance and for certain other terminal development.
3.	The development of harbours other than those administered by the national harbours board or local commissions will be the responsibility of the Department of Public Works, which I understand has the matter under review.
In reply to part 2, the program of works at Montreal harbour, estimated to cost $57 million, is being carried out. The St. Lawrence seaway authority is constructing 4,000 linear feet of wharf above the Cote Ste. Catherine lock. Other developments will receive consideration as the need arises.
As to part 3, no action has been taken to extend the jurisdiction of the national harbours board, but this matter will remain under review. The policy of the government will be to provide facilities when the public interest so requires.
The reply to part 4 is that a contract has been awarded for the construction of an additional commodious transit shed.
In answer to part 5 I would say that in the normal course the government will give consideration to recommendations of the national harbours board for such new facilities as the growth of traffic warrants.
Part 6 is answered by the reply to part 5.

Questions
As to part 7, the grain elevator at Three Rivers is privately owned and its capacity has recently been increased.
In reply to part 8 I might say that the Department of Public Works recently awarded a contract for improvements to the east face of terminal wharf No. 1 at Sorel amounting to $47,204. Surveys and pre-engineering studies are continuing in order to have available the necessary information for recommendations concerning future expansion or improvements.
The answer to part 9 is that the provision of cargo handling equipment, additional space on existing wharves and new docks will be considered by the Department of Public Works should the need for such additional facilities be justified. At present the facilities at the port of Sorel appear to be adequate.
Part 10 is answered by the reply to part 8.

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport):
maintopic: STARRED QUESTIONS
speechtext:
As to question 6, Mr. Speaker, the
answer to the first part is that the original cost was $18,571,308. With regard to the second part, the operating expenses between 1947 and 1956, inclusive, were $1,842,325. Profit and loss position shows a deficit as at December 31, 1946, of $11,439,297, and as at December 31, 1956, $9,338,148.
The answer to part 3 is yes, after litigation with respect to a portion.

As to part 4, the answer is that the province has paid in part and there remains unpaid $744,425, plus interest.
With regard to part 5, as the hon. member may be aware, the situation with respect to this matter has remained unchanged for several years. Directions were given in 1953, when he was minister of transport, that a petition of right be presented to the province of Quebec and a fiat sought. Accordingly the Department of Justice filed such petition, to which no response was received. The record does not indicate that any further action was taken to dispose of that matter.
The answer to part 6 is $22,670,794 to December 31, 1956.
With respect to part 7, as the hon. member knows there has been no change in the situation which existed while he was minister of transport, namely that the tripartite agreement, authorized by the statute of the province of Quebec, provided that the bridge shall be a toll bridge.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the Minister of Agriculture. What steps are being taken or what research is being done by the Department of Agriculture to check the insects that attack rape plants?

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of Agriculture):
maintopic: AGRICULTURE
subtopic: STATEMENT ON RESEARCH RESPECTING INSECTS ATTACKING RAPE PLANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank the hon. member for giving me notice of this question. Active research on the control of the insect pest species attacking rape is in progress at two science service laboratories in western Canada. Work formerly carried on at Brandon has now been transferred to the laboratory at Winnipeg. The Manitoba work has been confined to establishing the identity, distribution and abundance of the insect species involved leading up to a forecasting system. A more intensive program is being directed from the Saskatoon laboratory.
The bertha army worm is the most important pest of rape in Saskatchewan in recent years. Each year surveys are carried

out to forecast the abundance of moths and the potential of outbreaks and damage in each district. The Saskatoon laboratory uses radio, newspapers and direct contact with district agricultural representatives to inform farmers of the hazard. In districts where the infestation is likely to be severe special attention is paid to extension work via the agricultural representatives.
A satisfactory chemical control of bertha army worm has been developed. This involves the application by aeroplane of D.D.T. in diesel fuel oil at 10 ounces per acre in two to three quarts per acre. This control method is used extensively and is well known by both farmer operators and custom aircraft spray applicators. It is common practice for the custom applicators to be in constant touch with the Saskatoon laboratory and to keep supplies of the necessary materials on hand. Investigations are being continued on the potential usefulness of newer insecticides for the control of this pest.
Other insects of importance in rape production are the red backed cutworm, beet-webworm and the red turnip beetle. In Alberta some fields were destroyed by red backed cutworms in 1957, and this insect can be of importance if it occurs in outbreak proportions in Saskatchewan. Work is still in progress on the chemical control of beetweb-worm, and progress depends upon the availability of infestations suitable for field investigation. The red turnip beetle is of potential importance, particularly in the spring. No work is at present in progress at Saskatoon on the control of this insect on rape, but investigations carried on elsewhere have shown that effective control can be obtained with D.D.T.

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Tuesday, October 29, consideration in committee of Bill No. 14, to provide for advance payments for prairie grain prior to delivery thereof-Mr. Harkness (for Mr. Churchill)-Mr. Courtemanche in the chair.
On clause 1-Short title.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, ordinarily the practice in connection with these bills referring to agricultural matters has been to send them to the agriculture committee for study and consideration. We, of course, did not make that suggestion in connection with this bill because we did not want to hold up the proceedings of the house or the bringing into effect of the measure itself. But in so far as the general field of cash advances and agricultural policy are concerned, I think it would be greatly to the advantage of the members of this house, and to the agricultural industry of this country, if we could have a meeting of the agricultural committee during this session to discuss some aspects of a general agricultural program.
I wonder if the government has considered whether the wheat board officials might not be brought before the agriculture committee during the current session to give a report of their stewardship, and to allow members to inquire into the grain situation at this time. It seems to me there has been a very serious drop in export markets and grain sales. Grain prices, if anything, have been weaker in recent months. Furthermore, there is the whole question of procedure in regard to interim and final payments. I think that

Grain
when the agricultural industry is in such a bad way the minister and the government might give some consideration to having the agriculture committee meet to discuss the grain situation as well as the general agricultural situation in this country.
I wonder if the minister would care to say whether or not it is the intention of the government to have the agriculture committee meet during this session?

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the agriculture committee will be set up in due course and the government will be glad to give consideration to the request of the hon. member for Assiniboia with regard to having the officials of the wheat board appear before the committee for some discussion and investigation into the present grain situation.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext:
I did not speak on the second reading of this bill because I spoke during the resolution stage. Now that we are in committee, I should like to ask the minister to clarify one point. I have received some letters from individual farmers who are not too fascinated with this measure, if one can judge by the content of their letters. It appears that they may be under a misapprehension as to what it is going to cost to administer this measure. Of course, they assume it is going to cost something, and that the wheat board will have to pay it which, of course, means that the farmers of Canada as a whole will have to pay the shot whether or not they take advantage of it. In the house we have been given to understand that the administration costs, so far as the farmers are concerned, will be almost infinitesimal.
I wonder if the minister would care to make that point very clear? Perhaps he would rather wait until we are farther along with the bill, but if I can I should like to answer my farmers with regard to the cost in terms of the percentage of the cost of a bushel of wheat. If they think it is going to cost several million dollars, psychologically that seems like a lot of money. But if it is going to cost one-hundredth of a cent per bushel, that is infinitesimal. I wonder if the minister could inform the wheat growers on that particular point?

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext:
I would be glad to do so. I am sorry to learn there is any misapprehension in regard to these matters. I thought I had made it very clear when I spoke the day before yesterday in introducing this bill for second reading. The administration costs which will be incurred by the elevator companies in issuing cheques to farmers, and the necessity of having to take on extra staff in order to handle and process applications,

are going to be assumed by the elevator companies. The three western wheat pools, the United Grain Growers and the line elevator companies agreed to assume these administration costs which they, themselves, would be incurring in carrying out the administration of this measure. The administration costs which the wheat board will be paying are those which are concerned really with the issuing of forms, the printing of those forms and the extra staff required to process the forms when they are returned.
The administration costs of the elevator companies on the one hand, and the wheat board on the other, would be extremely difficult to sort out from their general administration costs and therefore it was felt- and these people agreed-that the most practical way to handle this matter was for the elevator companies to assume the administration costs that they incurred as a result of operating this scheme and the wheat board to do the same. These administration costs are not going to be large. I think the estimate of the wheat board so far as their administration costs are concerned is somewhere between $100,000 and $125,000.
I should like to point out to the hon. member that any talk about millions of dollars of costs so far as the wheat board or the farmers are concerned is incorrect. The only costs that the farmers will have any part in at all in connection with this legislation will be this amount estimated at $100,000 or $125,000. The hon. member will find in a subsequent clause that one of the methods by which the wheat board might meet these administration costs is dealt with.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext: Can we assume, then, Mr. Chairman, that the administration costs will amount to merely a fraction of a cent per bushel?

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman, it would be an extremely small fraction. As I say, the only costs the farmer will have any part in at all will be this $100,000 or $125,000 assumed by the wheat board.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext:
On that point, may I say that when my hon. friend suggests that these administration costs will not be very high, will that not depend a great deal on the responsibility which the policy of the government or the legislation itself places upon the elevator companies, whether they be pool or privately owned?
I would think that if the responsibility for losses is made to apply to those who are going to buy the grain, either they will have to go to considerable expense in order to make absolutely certain that they are not responsible for those losses or they will have

to be extremely careful about the advances they make. I should like to know just how that is going to be avoided. I should like to know how the placing of so much responsibility on the agent or on the elevator company is going to affect the amount of the advance that goes out.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I dealt with this matter fairly fully the day before yesterday when I indicated that the elevator companies have indicated their willingness to assume 10 per cent of the loss on any particular advance or on every advance that they make up to an over-all total of one-quarter of one per cent of all the advance which result from loans that any particular company made. That was arrived at as an amount which would give them a sense of responsibility in making the advance. It was considered that it was sufficient for that purpose so that the agents or the elevator companies would not, we will say, enter into wild competition with one another to put out advances. At the same time it is not sufficient so that it is going to impose a heavy burden on the elevator companies.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think it has been said that as a result of this bill providing for cash advances to the western farmer $100 million to $150 million a year would become available to the farmers of the west. I think this will strengthen our economy in the east as well. I think it was stated in the speech from the throne that all farmers will get a fair share of our national income. I hope this promise will be carried out in connection with the primary producers in the other seven provinces. I live in the Niagara district. We have much fruit there. Often the fruit rots on the ground and because of marketing conditions and because of the lack of storage the farmers there cannot dispose of their fruit. I hope they will get the same consideration as is being given to the western farmers. I may say that I support this bill in the hope that the farmers of Ontario, the fruit growers of the Niagara district and farmers everywhere, for that matter, will get similar consideration.
There was just one point in connection with this bill which I do not think was brought out. Government members and other members of the house said that this was emergency legislation. If this is emergency legislation, why does the government not treat it as such and put a time limit on the bill of, say, 12 months to 18 months? It seems to me that we cannot here assess the needs of the farmers of the west three or four years from now.
Grain
I recall that the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Trade and Commerce criticized us severely because our government was not selling more wheat. I think it is fair to say now that they are selling considerably less wheat then we were selling last year.
I refer to the fact that the Minister of Trade and Commerce went to England, presumably to sell wheat. At that time Britain placed an order with the United States for a considerable shipment of wheat. I certainly do not think the Minister of Trade and Commerce was very successful in selling wheat on that particular trip. I hope he is more successful in the future. I also sincerely hope that our government will make every effort to come to a better understanding with the United States with regard to their methods of wheat marketing so that they will not put us at any disadvantage in our wheat marketing. Certainly we have traditional markets and it seems to me that the United States are making inroads into those markets.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext: I am glad to hear the hon. member for Welland say he thinks that this legislation will be of general benefit throughout Canada. I am sure that it will. I do not want any misapprehension, however, to be left in the mind of anyone that $100 million or $150 million is being given to the western farmers.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext: I did not say that.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext:
I know that the hon. member for Welland did not say that but he mentioned $150 million. I want to make sure that there is no misapprehension along that line. This money is being put out in the form of an advance. We expect that the average length of time that it will be out before it is returned is about six months.
In view of the statements which were made in this house yesterday and the day before by some hon. members, particularly the member for Quebec-Montmorency, I think the impression may have been sent abroad that $100 million or $150 million was being given to the farmers of western Canada.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext: I did not mean to imply that.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext:
I know that. I know that the hon. member for Welland did not say that. However, as I say, some other hon. members yesterday made statements which would leave that impression. I want to make it absolutely clear that no such thing is contemplated or is going to take place.
The hon. member for Welland asked why there was no time limit on the bill if it is emergency legislation. The reason there is no time limit on it is that we believe this

Grain
legislation should remain on the statute books and be available whenever there arises a situation such as the one we have at the present time. A situation such as this has arisen before. In fact, we have had it for the past three or four years. I refer to the inability of the farmers to deliver their grain in the fall of the year and a consequent shortage of cash. With the amount of surplus wheat we have at the present time there is no question that we are going to have difficulty along that line for at least the next couple of years. That is why there is no time limit on the bill. It is needed not only this year but it will be needed next year, and it may be needed at various times in the future. We therefore think it should not have a time limit but should remain on the statute books.
There was one other thing I wished to mention. The hon. member made a statement which was made yesterday and which I refuted yesterday, namely that we are selling much less wheat than did the previous government. I put the figures on the record yesterday and I am not going to repeat them. On clause 6 Mr. Chairman, I have certain amendments which I would ask my colleague, the Minister of National Defence, to move. Clause 6 will be amended by making the present clause 6 "Clause 6, subsection (1)" and adding the following new subsections:
(2)	An application by two or more producers may specify the shares of the advance payment to be paid to each.
(3)	Where an application by two or more joint producers specifies the share of the advance payment to be paid to each such producer, and subsequently the undertaking is in default, a joint producer who pays to the board an amount that is in the same proportion to the amount in default as his share of the advance payment is to the total advance payment, together with interest thereon at the rate of 6 per cent per annum after default, is, notwithstanding anything in this act, relieved of his obligation to make any further payment to the board in respect of the default.
I might say in explanation of that that the purpose of the amendment is to relieve a joint producer from his obligation on default to pay more than his proportionate share of the balance of the money due.
The landlord is entitled to one-third of the crop and therefore he is entitled to one-third of the advance. You may have the sort of situation where, we will say, an advance of $1,500 is given of which the landlord receives $500. The tenant might then by some dishonest means dispose of the 3,000 bushels of grain against which that advance has been made. It would be impossible for

him to deliver and the tenant after dishonestly disposing of the grain might depart from the country.
Under the provision as it existed it could have been possible that the landlord in such a case would have become liable for the whole $1,500 advance which had been made which of course would not have been fair and equitable. Therefore this amendment has been introduced to ensure that in the case of a joint producer of that sort, whether he be c landlord or any one else, he will not be liable for the repayment of more than the amount he receives initially in the event default does take place. I might say further that if this amendment had not been put in it might well have been that a considerable number of landlords would not have been prepared to sign applications and tenants would thus have been precluded from securing these cash advances. To ensure to the extent that we can that all tenants would be able to secure these cash advances we are moving this amendment.

There are some good and simple reasons why permit books are applied for jointly. One is that the income tax department, I am told, uses Canadian wheat board records in the initial stages and also for subsequent payments in determining or assessing a farmer's tax. The other reason, of course, is that it facilitates distribution of subsequent wheat board payments. That is the reason why many permit books are taken out jointly. I can see that this clause would possibly be workable in the case of individuals, landlord and tenant, and so on. Where two or more producers are entitled to deliver grain under one permit book, no advance payment shall be made unless all such producers named in the permit book jointly make the application and execute the undertaking-
I know that some of these municipal governments are hard pressed for money but I do not think they would be willing to undertake a joint application with an individual farmer for these advances.
When the permit books are taken out the elevator agent usually asks you this question: "Is there anyone else interested in the grain or crop that is growing on the land that is specified in the permit book?" And when you tell him that there is someone else such as the department of lands and forests, special areas, or some other individual, then it becomes a joint permit book; but in practice, when you go to sell grain with this permit book there is no specific share designated and any one party can sell anywhere from one per cent to 100 per cent of the grain. Certainly, it would appear to me that if we leave this section in the bill then, unless those governments and other parties I have mentioned are willing to undertake to execute the application jointly the tenants are certainly going to be precluded.
In looking it over and being familiar with the practical application of what happens when there is a joint permit book, I would like to recommend to the minister that until and unless some changes are made in applying for a permit book so that in that permit book there are definite shares designated when you take it out he should delete this clause altogether.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we cannot delete the clause altogether because this system would not work. In regard to the difficulties which are envisaged by the hon. member, I would say to him that anyone who has an interest in the delivery of the grain, or in the proceeds from the grain which has been grown on that farm, becomes a joint signer of the application and is classed with the producer and therefore his claims are protected in that way. If he does not want to take any advance all he has to do is sign the agreement with the tenant, we will say, on the farm getting the advance. He does not have to take any advance himself if he does not want to and then he would have no liability for repayment if a default took place.
The way the system will work is that the cheques will be made out jointly, if it is requested in the application that that be done; or it may be requested in the application and specified that the cheques will be

made out individually, we will say, two-thirds to the tenant and one-third to the landlord if the landlord has a one-third interest in the grain grown and the tenant two-thirds. Therefore, I think the difficulties which were envisaged by the hon. member were all looked after either in the legislation itself or they will be in the regulations which will be drawn up as provided for in this legislation.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext: I can see that in the repayment the share is designated; but it seems to me that if we leave this in here and if there are some landlords who are either unwilling, or unavailable to the elevator agent, to sign the application the tenant will not be able to take advantage of this unless he can obtain his signature in the first instance when applying for the advance.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext: It is quite true, Mr. Chairman, that if the landlord refuses to sign the application the tenant will not be able to secure cash advances; but it is essential that the landlord, or whoever else has an interest and right to secure a share of the grain produced on that land, sign the application otherwise the scheme would fall through.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext: I should like to make one point on this because for some years past I have represented unpaid vendors, people who have retired off the land and sold their land on a crop-share basis. There have been far too many occasions where those people have been left completely at the mercy of the purchaser as to whether payment was made or not. The excuse was always that the grain was not marketed. I feel that here is an opportunity for those people. I can assure hon. members that the cases of hardship in that instance are almost as difficult as those who bought land or who are tenants on the land. Many of those people are old and sick and they now have an opportunity to get some of the money to which they are entitled. I feel that this is a method by which they can get protection- they have notice-when the advance payments are made; otherwise they might not, because hon. members will see in other sections of the bill provision is made for liens on the grain and one thing and another. The grain is completely dissipated and they must wait another year. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I would suggest that the wording of the clause remain as it is.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext:
May I say a
word on that? From what the minister said a moment ago it seems to me that there may be considerable difficulty as a result of this clause. The minister indicated a moment
Grain
ago that if there were a landlord and a tenant the landlord might be entitled to one-third and the tenant to two-thirds of the cash advances. But in the case where the landlord refused to sign the permit book, no matter how urgent the need was for the tenant to get his share of the cash advance, he would be prevented from getting it. It would seem to me it would be rather easy to have an amendment to this section as to permit the tenant to get at least his two-thirds of the cash advance whether or not the landlord wished to take advantage of his one-third; otherwise you could get a landlord who might say to his tenant, "Well I do not need this money; I am just not going to sign away my right."
I can understand quite well that this may happen. If the landlord happens to be ornery, let us say, the tenant is put in such a position that he would not get any relief under this legislation no matter how greatly he needed it. I would think that the minister should have another look at this. Possibly he could let the clause stand until tomorrow and see if it cannot be amended in such a way as to relieve this difficulty. If it has to go through this way then it will have to but if this situation can be relieved in any way I think that every effort should be made to amend the clause in order to avoid this predicament.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. member for Bow River is labouring under fears which are not justified. There is no advantage to the landlord in refusing to sign the application and there are considerable advantages to him in signing it. By signing the application he loses absolutely nothing and cannot lose anything. On the other hand, he gets his share of the crop and really his only interest in the land is to get his share of the crop. He gets paid for part of his share of the crop immediately instead of having to wait several months for payment. That immediately reduces his risk and it gives him money in hand which he can use for other purposes. It is all to his advantage to sign the application. Now that this amendment has been introduced so that there is no chance of him having any liability for any money except the money he actually receives I do not see any reason why he would not sign. Why should he refuse to sign? Self-interest and everything else, particularly his interest in keeping on good terms with his tenant, would all lead him to sign. I do not think the hon. member needs to be afraid on this point at all.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext:
It might be that no trouble would arise but I think there would be instances where the landlord just would

Grain
not sign and under those circumstances I cannot see why it would do any harm at all to include a clause that would protect the tenant. As the minister says, it would appear that everything would be in the interest of the landlord to sign but there are landlords who just do not want to sign these things no matter whether it seems to be to their advantage to do so. In that case the tenant would be penalized and I do not think that should be allowed.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext: The simple answer as to why it cannot be done is that if you tried to do it in that way and give the tenant an advance on the two-thirds of the grain which he is entitled to deliver and to get the initial price for, you would have to segregate the grain. In other words, you would have to go back into the business of sending somebody out to the farm to see that the grain was segregated on the farm and take only security on the two-thirds share which belonged to the tenant and leave out the one-third share which belonged to the landlord. It would make the thing impractical and, as I pointed out before, I cannot see any reason in the world why the landlord would refuse to sign. The advantage is all to him if he does sign.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext: Could the minister tell us what would be the effect on an application under this section if a producer happened to die after the permit book was issued and before the advance was made?

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext: The legal adviser tells me that the executor of his estate would then sign the application.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext: I expect, of course, that that would be the case after the executor or administrator of the estate is appointed, but quite frequently there is an interregnum due to many causes. Could some provision be made either here or in the issuing of permits to cover that situation?

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext: Well, the length of the interregnum would probably not be long in most cases and if there was a real emergency to secure cash he could always act under the Bank Act.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the tenant has
an interest in the grain and I certainly cannot go along with the idea, if we are going to make cash advances available to people who have an interest in grain stored on farms, that the tenant, in order to obtain an advance must be dependent on whether or not his landlord will permit him to do so or will sign his application with him. Inasmuch as the tenant has the grain he should be able to go individually and get his advance. If

this clause is going to be left in the legislation, then I think the minister should give serious consideration to making some changes in the application for a permit book so that it will clearly designate the shares of the tenant and the landlord in the grain because then the amount of the advance could be determined in accordance with the shares so designated.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext:
This clause reads:
Where the board has made an advance payment to a producer, the board has a lien for the amount thereof on the grain in respect of which the advance payment was made.
A question arises here as to whether the lien will be on all the grain the farmer has in storage or whether it will be just on the six bushels per acre quota. The minister has mentioned that the hail lien will take precedence over this lien and I was wondering whether or not some of these provincial liens, municipal tax liens and other provincial liens would take precedence over this lien for the advance. What will actually happen is that the farmer will get these cash advances and he will just pay off his liens. He will not have any more cash than he had when he started.
Not only will that be the case, but if the lien covers all the grain held on the farm he will not be able to sell grain or obtain a further loan from a bank. Let us say a farmer has a ten bushel to the acre crop. He will not be able to get a loan on the amount over the 6-bushel quota. I think that word "grain" should be qualified to mean the amount of grain this lien actually covers.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext: It covers the grain on which the advance is made. In other words, if a man has secured an advance of $3,000 on a security of 6,000 bushels of grain, that is what is covered and that is the grain on which the lien exists.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext:
Supposing a man has 10,000 bushels and he is able to get an advance on only 6,000 bushels. There has never been any separation made of the grain and perhaps he has the 10,000 bushels in one pile or in one bin. Unless there has been a separation of the grain, is the lien on the whole
10.000	bushels or is it only on some portion of it that is not designated?

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext:
It is on the 6,000 bushels. From a practical point of view, this is the situation. If he had 10,000 bushels, he would be at liberty to take 4,000 bushels out and feed it or sell it or do anything else with it. But if he takes out some of the 6,000 bushels, in other words, if he gets down below the
6.000	bushels then he becomes liable for the penalties mentioned here because he has been selling some of the grain on which he has obtained an advance.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext:
Assuming he needs an advance on the other 4,000 bushels, is the whole
10.000	bushels tied up in such a way that he cannot go to the bank and get an advance on the other 4,000?

No, he would be at liberty to segregate the grain himself if he wanted to. So far as the wheat board is concerned, if he has taken an advance on 6,000 bushels of grain, in other words taken an advance of $3,000, the board has a lien on 6,000 bushels of grain. 4,000	bushels over and above the 6,000 on which the advance has been made and which are security for that advance.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext: I am not worrying about either the wheat board or the banks, for that matter, or any other person, but here is a man who owns 130,000 bushels of grain which is in one pile on the prairie. I know many who may have 20,000 bushels in that way, and if a man is not able to deliver his wheat, if he is in difficulties, and he can be -it is all very well for some of my friends to say that he is not in much trouble if he has that much wheat; sometimes a man who is in that position is in more trouble than the person to whom he owes money-if he does get an advance, whether he has 12,000 bushels or 14,000 bushels, then he is not able to go to the bank and borrow against that amount which is over and above the amount covered by the lien. He is not able to borrow until he has cleared up the whole situation with the wheat board.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman, anyone v/ho has 20,000 or 30,000 bushels of wheat will never get into any trouble under this measure. He will always have the 6,000 bushels which acts as security for the $3,000 he has had as an advance. What he does with the remainder of it is his own business.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext: But after he has cleared up his business with you? You go to the bank with that lien and see how much money you will get.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext: We have made an advance on the 6,000 bushels, and what he does with the rest is his business. If he can get a loan from a bank or from anywhere else, it is all right; it is his business.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext: Does this lien take priority over the liens for municipal taxes or some of the other liens we have in the province of Alberta?

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we believe that we have got around all the difficulties in connection with liens, such as thresher liens, hail insurance liens, municipal tax liens and so forth, by providing when the advance is issued that it will be dealt with

Grain
in exactly the same way as if the farmer had delivered the grain and received his initial payment on it.
As hon. members know, out in our country each elevator agent has a list of the farmers' names, and under each name he has a notation of the liens which are against that man. If there is a municipal tax lien of $200 and the farmer comes in with a big load of wheat, for which he is to receive $400, the elevator agent gives him $200 in cash and the other $200 he pays to the municipal district to cover the taxes. Exactly the same thing will happen in so far as these advances are concerned. When a farmer comes in to obtain a cash advance, the elevator agent looks at his list just the same as he would if the farmer were delivering wheat. Then the agent pays him off accordingly and the persons who had liens are thereby looked after. When it comes to the actual delivery of the grain, these lien holders have no claim against that particular grain on which the advance was made because they have already been paid.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext: I am not quite clear on this. For example, in the municipality from which I come a farmer must pay his taxes by the end of November. Suppose he has already obtained a cash advance and at the end of November he does not pay his taxes. The municipality sends out the sheriff to seize the grain. Now, which lien has priority, this lien or the municipal tax lien?

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext: If the wheat board lien were taken out first, which would be the case, it would have priority over the subsequent lien.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext: I understand that in the province of Alberta the municipal tax liens come before any other liens.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext: Actually, in the province of Alberta they do not, they come after threshers' and several others.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext:
I am afraid the minister is treating this legislation in the way one would treat any piece of legislation that simply deals with selling something upon which there is a lien. However, that is not the purpose of this legislation. The purpose of this legislation is to make cash available to the farmer. These liens which are filed with the elevator agents, in most cases, represent more than the farmer would receive from these advances. A lot has been said about the average amount of the loans that were obtained under the interim financing act. They averaged around $600, $700 or $800, but the farmer will not obtain any more under this measure. The other day the

minister put figures on Hansard to indicate that most of the farms are small farms, and the average farmer will not be able to get more than that amount under this legislation.
He goes to the elevator and the first thing that is taken out is an amount for his taxes. In many cases that can be $400 or $500. Then if there are some other liens in addition they are taken out and he is sent home without any money at all. That is not the objective of this legislation. The objective of it is not to pay the accounts that the man could pay if he had marketed his crop, the object of the legislation is to put some cash in his hands so that he can carry on until such time as he can deliver his grain and get cash, and that means going to the merchants in the village with whom he deals and paying cash for what he buys. He cannot pay cash if he has paid it all out in taxes which were overdue and so on. I suggest this provision limits the benefits far more than I had hoped it would.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext:
When I was speaking the other day I made reference to the unfair position in which the farmer was going to find himself. I had special reference to section 18 of the act. However, I see now that it also applies to this section 10, as has just been pointed out by the former minister of agriculture, the hon. member for Melville. I pointed out the same difficulty yesterday when I was speaking, namely that this legislation was primarily intended to give assistance to the farmer to pay those bills which are most urgent, such as a grocery bill or a doctor bill, to buy clothes for the kiddies and so on. This legislation is not going to give him that advantage. Not only are the liens or taxes to have priority but the government itself has priority if the farmer has borrowed under the Prairie Grain Producers Interim Financing Act.
If you take out all these obligations that have been piling up on the farmer back over all these years,-if he has any arrears of taxes; if he has borrowed money under the Prairie Grain Producers' Interim Financing Act and if he owes other obligations which have liens attached to them-then the farmer is not going to get anything at all out of this advance.
As the minister pointed out to us the other day,-and I referred to the matter yesterday, -about two-thirds of the farmers of the western prairies have about 300 acres or less which will qualify for this advance. That means that they are not going to get more than about $900 at the most. When you take out the obligations where he has given security by liens, the farmer is just not going to have anything to take home with which

to pay the groceryman or the butcher or to buy much needed clothes for his family for this winter.
Surely that was not the intention of the act. When the minister was speaking the other day on this bill he went on at some great length to point out how urgently this money was needed by the farmers at this time because they could not pay their bills, and he said this legislation is going to be of great help to them. Now the minister says that the farmer is just being placed in the same position as that in which he would be placed if he were getting his initial payment. That is not true at all. If he were getting his initial payment, he would be getting $1.40 and he would have some money to do something with. But here he is going to get only 50 cents. There is a great deal of difference between 50 cents and $1.40.
If the government really intended that this legislation was to be of some assistance to these farmers who now find themselves in need of some cash, surely they should give the farmers some consideration in this regard and these liens should not have priority over this cash advance. I am not suggesting for a moment that the farmer should get out from under his obligations. However, I am suggesting most emphatically that he should have an opportunity to provide for his family first. I want to make that point clear. This is an emergency. It is something that has arisen. The farmer is just desperate. Surely we are not going to allow this so-called emergent measure to deprive the farmer of the opportunity of buying those necessities for his family and of paying the proprietor of the small grocery store or the small butcher shop or those others who have been financing him over this period. If something is not done we are going to find that many of the farmers will be disappointed in this legislation.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext:
The logical end of the sort of argument we have just been hearing would be that there is no advantage at all to the farmer in being able to deliver his crop because he owes debts and as he delivers his crop in the normal course of events the
Grain
debts that he owes are subtracted from his deliveries by the elevator agent. That is the logical end of this argument, namely that if he has debts there is no advantage to the farmer in delivering his crop, that he might just as well not deliver it. This argument really is that there is no advantage in his delivering half his crop, because essentially that is what he is doing, or at least he is getting paid, we will say, on the basis of delivering half or as though he had delivered half his crop. The advance payment, in the average case, will amount to approximately one-half of what he would have got if he had been able to deliver the whole six-bushel quota which we expect is the amount the farmers will be able to deliver this year.
The hon. member's argument simply amounts to a statement that if the farmer has debts there is no advantage to him in delivering grain. I just cannot see why anyone should carry on an argument of that kind. Inevitably where it leads you is to the conclusion that if the farmer has debts he should be given an advance whether he has debts or not and that his debtors should be just forgotten about. I do not think you can do that, particularly when the debtors are probably the people who threshed for him, the people who gave him hail insurance, the municipal district to which he pays taxes and so on.
